Brooklyn Latin

Main article: [Brooklyn Latin School](/wiki/Brooklyn_Latin_School "Brooklyn Latin School")

Unlike nearly all other specialized high schools, Brooklyn Latin has a strong focus on the humanities and classics. All students are required to take four years of English, History, Latin, and a modern foreign language. All classes regularly hold Socratic Seminars, in which students lead roundtable question-and-answer discussions, and all students take part in declamation (public speaking) exercises. Because of its small class size, Brooklyn Latin offers a relatively low student-to-teacher ratio (currently around 16:1). All students are required to take [International Baccalaureate](/wiki/International_Baccalaureate "International Baccalaureate") courses in junior and senior years.

fanoutqa_036375.t: List of tallest trees :: Maximum limits of tree height :: chunk_0003
fanoutqa_036375.x:
List of tallest trees :: Maximum limits of tree height :: chunk_0003
Two main opposing forces affect a [tree](/wiki/Tree "Tree")'s height; one pushes it upward while the other holds it down. By analyzing the interplay between these forces in coast redwoods (*Sequoia sempervirens*), a team of biologists led by George Koch of [Northern Arizona University](/wiki/Northern_Arizona_University "Northern Arizona University") calculated the theoretical maximum tree height or the point at which opposing forces balance out and a tree stops growing. This point lies somewhere between 122 and 130 m (400 and 427 ft).[[51]](#cite_note-52) On the one hand, the researchers found, trees in forests "desire" to grow as tall as possible to overtake neighboring trees and reach stronger sunlight. On the other hand, gravity makes it more and more difficult to haul water upwards from the roots to the [canopy](/wiki/Canopy_(biology) "Canopy (biology)") as the tree grows, and [leaves](/wiki/Leaf "Leaf") thus become smaller near the top. They discovered that despite the moistness of the ground far below, the leaves at the treetops struggle to get enough water, so they are effectively living in a constant drought. The difficulty of getting [water](/wiki/Water "Water") so far up into the sky is what ultimately constrains growth.[[52]](#cite_note-53) Other researchers have developed models of maximum height for Coast Douglas-fir (*Pseudotsuga menziesii var. menziesii*) trees that yield similar estimates of 109 to 138 meters (358 to 453 ft),[[53]](#cite_note-:1-54) a range that includes the height of the tallest reliably-measured historical (dead) specimen, a 126-meter tree.[[53]](#cite_note-:1-54)[[54]](#cite_note-55)[[55]](#cite_note-56)

[Braj Kachru](/wiki/Braj_Kachru "Braj Kachru") has categorised countries into the [Three Circles of English](/wiki/Three_Circles_of_English "Three Circles of English") model, according to how the language historically spread in each country, how it is acquired by the populace, and the range of uses it has there – with a country's classification able to change over time.[[73]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKachru2006196-73)[[74]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESvartvikLeech20062-74)

"Inner-circle" countries have large communities of native English speakers; these include the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, Canada, Ireland, and New Zealand, where the majority speaks English – and South Africa, where a significant minority speaks English. Denmark became a member of the European Union in 1973 and signed the [Lisbon Treaty](/wiki/Lisbon_Treaty "Lisbon Treaty") in 2007.

Denmark was a founding member of the [European Free Trade Association](/wiki/European_Free_Trade_Association "European Free Trade Association") (EFTA). During the 1960s, the EFTA countries were often referred to as the [Outer Seven](/wiki/Outer_Seven "Outer Seven"), as opposed to the [Inner Six](/wiki/Inner_Six "Inner Six") of what was then the [European Economic Community](/wiki/European_Economic_Community "European Economic Community") (EEC).[[59]](#cite_note-68) In 1973, along with Britain and Ireland, Denmark joined the European Economic Community (now the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union")) after a [public referendum](/wiki/1972_Danish_European_Communities_membership_referendum "1972 Danish European Communities membership referendum"). The [Maastricht Treaty](/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty "Maastricht Treaty"), which involved further European integration, [was rejected](/wiki/1992_Danish_Maastricht_Treaty_referendum "1992 Danish Maastricht Treaty referendum") by the Danish people in 1992; it was only accepted after a [second referendum](/wiki/1993_Danish_Maastricht_Treaty_referendum "1993 Danish Maastricht Treaty referendum") in 1993, which provided for [four opt-outs](/wiki/Opt-outs_in_the_European_Union "Opt-outs in the European Union") from policies. The Danes rejected the euro as the national currency in [a referendum in 2000](/wiki/2000_Danish_euro_referendum "2000 Danish euro referendum"). The [Older Parthenon](/wiki/Older_Parthenon "Older Parthenon") (in black) was destroyed by the Achaemenids during the [Destruction of Athens](/wiki/Destruction_of_Athens "Destruction of Athens") in 480–479 BC, and then rebuilt by [Pericles](/wiki/Pericles "Pericles") (in grey).

The first endeavour to build a sanctuary for [Athena Parthenos](/wiki/Athena#Athena_Parthenos:_Virgin_Athena "Athena") on the site of the present Parthenon was begun shortly after the [Battle of Marathon](/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon "Battle of Marathon") (c. 490–488 BC) upon a solid [limestone](/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") foundation that extended and levelled the southern part of the [Acropolis](/wiki/Acropolis "Acropolis") summit. This building replaced a [Hekatompedon temple](/wiki/Hekatompedon_temple "Hekatompedon temple") ("hundred-footer") and would have stood beside the [archaic temple dedicated to *Athena Polias*](/wiki/Old_Temple_of_Athena "Old Temple of Athena") ("of the city"). The [Older or Pre-Parthenon](/wiki/Older_Parthenon "Older Parthenon"), as it is frequently called, was still under construction when the [Persians](/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire") sacked the city in 480 BC and razed the Acropolis.[[51]](#cite_note-venieri-acropolis-51)[[52]](#cite_note-52)

The existence of both the proto-Parthenon and its destruction were known from [Herodotus](/wiki/Herodotus "Herodotus"),[[53]](#cite_note-53) and the drums of its columns were visibly built into the curtain wall north of the [Erechtheion](/wiki/Erechtheion "Erechtheion"). Main article: [Eagles–Steelers rivalry](/wiki/Eagles%E2%80%93Steelers_rivalry "Eagles–Steelers rivalry")

The [Philadelphia Eagles](/wiki/Philadelphia_Eagles "Philadelphia Eagles") and Steelers are both located in [Pennsylvania](/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") and began play in 1933. From that season through 1966, this was a major rivalry for both teams, as both were part of the same division. In 1967, they were placed in separate divisions, but remained in the same conference for three years. In 1970 the Steelers (along with the [Cleveland Browns](/wiki/Cleveland_Browns "Cleveland Browns") and [Baltimore Colts](/wiki/Baltimore_Colts "Baltimore Colts")) moved to the [American Football Conference](/wiki/American_Football_Conference "American Football Conference"), while the Eagles stayed with the rest of the old-line NFL teams in the [National Football Conference](/wiki/National_Football_Conference "National Football Conference"). As a result, the Eagles and Steelers no longer played each other every year; instead, they are scheduled to meet once every four years in the regular season. The most recent meeting was in 2024 at Lincoln Financial Field, a game in which the Eagles won 27–13. The Steelers have lost 11 straight games on the road against the Eagles dating back to 1966, which was also the start of the [Super Bowl](/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") era. The Eagles lead the all-time series 50–29–3.[[129]](#cite_note-130)
